4minut04.seo: How to Calm Down Quickly: A 4-Minute Eyes-Open Meditation
4minut04.desc: How to calm down quickly, even in a busy place: a 4-minute guided meditation with your eyes open, anchored to one object, your feet and a single sound. Free.
4minut04.h1: How to calm down quickly when everything moves too fast
4minut04.lead: Here is how to calm down quickly when everything speeds up. Let your eyes, your feet and your ears bring you back to the room. This 4-minute guided meditation walks you through it with your eyes open, wherever you are. There is nothing to fight and nothing to fix.

sections.h2: How to calm down quickly, step by step
p: The session, called “When Everything Moves Too Fast”, opens by letting whatever you feel be there. You don’t push it away. Your eyes can stay open from start to finish.

First, you look. You choose one object and notice its color, then one precise detail. Then a second object, then a third. Silently, you tell yourself where you are, what day it is and what time it is.

Next, you feel. Your feet press gently into the floor. You find three more points of contact: your back against the chair, your legs on the seat and your hands on your clothes. The breath comes in and flows out on its own.

Then your eyes get something steady to hold. You choose a horizontal line, such as the edge of a table or a shelf, and trace it slowly from end to end. After that, you listen for a single sound and return to your feet.
It ends with a short formula to keep for later: an object, a sound and your feet. You can listen to the session in the player above.

sections.h2: Why give your attention something concrete?
p: When life speeds up, the mind speeds up with it. Thoughts rush ahead, and everything seems urgent at once. Arguing with them rarely slows them down.

This session takes a different approach. It lets the thoughts run in the background and hands your attention something slower to hold. An object, the floor and a single sound all belong to the here and now. None of them asks you to solve anything.
This is what people often call grounding: coming back to the room through your senses. Your breath is never forced. Calm is allowed to return at its own pace, without a deadline.

sections.h2: How to relieve anxiety quickly, wherever you are
p: There is no switch that turns anxiety off. What you can change quickly is where your attention rests. That is why this 4-minute meditation keeps your eyes open.

Use it at your desk, on a bus or just before a meeting. It works well as a discreet meditation at work, since it only asks you to look, feel and listen. Sit with your feet flat on the floor if you can. Standing works too, as long as you feel the ground.
Headphones help in a noisy place, but one earbud is enough. No experience is needed, since this is a beginner session.

sections.h2: What if the wave comes back?
p: Calm does not always return in one go. A wave can rise again after a minute. The session expects this. You go back to one point of contact, such as your feet or your hands, and let the wave pass.
Your mind may also run off toward what is waiting for you. That is normal. Come back to the next object, the next sound or the floor. Each return counts, even if it lasts only a second.
If an emotion comes up, you don’t have to name it or explain it. The opening of the session already lets it be there. With your eyes open, you stay in the room the whole time.

sections.h2: Two quick meditations to try next
p: To let go of tension in the body, try “Relax Very Quickly”. In three minutes, it relaxes the body area by area, from forehead to feet. If a conflict set you off, “Calming Down After an Argument” helps you step back before you reply.
Both are in the same 4 Minutes category. Like every session in MeditaDream, they are free, with no ads and no account.

faq: How can I calm myself down quickly?

Bring your attention to something concrete and still. In this session, that means one object, your feet on the floor and one sound in the room. Let the breath come and go on its own while the thoughts run in the background. Going through it once takes four minutes.
How do I calm my anxiety in public?

Keep your eyes open and use what is around you. Look at one object, feel your feet and pick out one sound. To anyone nearby, you are simply looking around. This session was made for those moments, on a bus, in a store or at your desk.
Do I have to close my eyes?

No. The whole session is designed for open eyes. You look at objects and lines in the room, so it works in places where closing your eyes would feel strange. Open eyes also keep you in touch with the room the whole time.
Is this guided meditation for anxiety free?
Yes. MeditaDream is free, with no ads and no account. Download the session once and it plays offline, so it is ready on your phone the next time everything moves too fast.

4minut06.seo: Meditation and Anger: 3-Minute Meditation After an Argument
4minut06.desc: Meditation and anger, in practice: a 3-minute meditation for right after an argument. Loosen your body, quiet the replay and decide once you’ve cooled down.
4minut06.h1: Meditation and anger: three minutes to cool down after an argument
4minut06.lead: Meditation and anger can go together, as long as the goal is not to make the anger disappear. This 3-minute session, made for right after an argument, opens a short pause between what you feel and what you do next. You loosen your body, quiet the replay and save the decision for later.

sections.h2: A 3-minute meditation after an argument, step by step
p: The session, “Calming Down After an Argument”, starts by setting aside who was right. Each time the scene starts playing again, you bring your attention back to your feet on the floor. Then you turn to what your body is feeling.
You look for the tightest place. You let the feeling stay and simply ease that spot a little. Your breath keeps its own rhythm.
Words will come back, theirs and the ones you wish you had said. To each replay, you give the same short answer: “Not now.” It does not mean never. It does not mean the argument is unimportant.

Next, you picture the same scene a few hours from now, when the anger has weakened. You ask what will still matter by then, and what was mostly the anger talking. You don’t need a full answer. You can also watch the scene the way you would watch someone else’s argument.

Then you separate three things: what you feel, what you think and what you decide to do. You notice which one is taking over and give it a one-word name. To finish, you relax your jaw, your hands and your shoulders.

sections.h2: Can meditation help with anger?
p: Meditation does not erase anger, and this session never tries to. Its central idea is simple. You can still be angry and wait before you reply or decide.
That pause matters because anger tends to fuse everything into one urge. Feeling, thought and decision arrive as a single block. Pulling them apart for a moment shows you which one is driving.

Distance helps too. Seen from a few hours ahead, or through someone else’s eyes, the scene can look smaller. That does not erase what happened. You can come back to the conversation once it has cooled down a few degrees.

sections.h2: When to use this quick meditation
p: Use it right after the argument, or as soon as you can be alone for three minutes. A hallway, a parked car or a quiet corner is enough. If you are wondering how to calm down after an argument, this is a simple place to start.
Sit or stand with your feet on the floor. Your eyes can stay open, since the session keeps bringing you back to what is around you. Headphones are optional. They help most in a noisy place.
It also works as a meditation at work, after a tense meeting or a sharp email. It is a beginner session, so no experience is needed.

sections.h2: What if the anger flares up again?
p: It probably will, at least once. The replay is stubborn. Each time, you return to your feet and then to the room. Once more, you tell yourself “not now.”

Your body may stay tense even when your thoughts slow down. Loosening a little is enough. Under the anger, you may find hurt or tiredness. Let that be there too. You don’t have to sort it all out in three minutes.
If you are still replaying an argument in your head an hour later, play the session again. The conversation can wait until you are ready.

sections.h2: Which session should you try next?
p: If the whole day feels too fast, try the session “When Everything Moves Too Fast”. It grounds you with your eyes open, through an object, your feet and a sound. If you keep guessing what others think of you, the session “When You Feel Watched or Judged” sorts what you know from what you imagine.
Both last four minutes and belong to the same 4 Minutes category.

faq: What should I do right after an argument?

Give yourself a short pause before replying. In this session, you set aside who was right and loosen the tightest spot in your body. Then you look at the scene from a few hours ahead. You can return to the conversation later, once the heat has dropped.
Is it okay to meditate while I’m still angry?

Yes. You don’t need to be calm to start. This guided meditation for anger is made for the first minutes, while you are still fuming. It never asks you to stop feeling angry. It only asks you to wait before you decide or reply.
How long does it take?
Three minutes. It is one of the shortest sessions in MeditaDream. If the first round is not enough, play it a second time, or follow it with another short session from the 4 Minutes category.
Is this meditation free?
Yes. MeditaDream is free, with no ads and no account. Once downloaded, the session plays offline, so it is ready on your phone the next time an argument leaves you shaken.

buddhi02.seo: Guanyin Bodhisattva: A Buddhist Compassion Meditation
buddhi02.desc: Guanyin Bodhisattva, also called Avalokiteśvara, guides this Buddhist compassion meditation of about 22 minutes: one situation, seen through eleven faces.
buddhi02.h1: Meditating with Guanyin Bodhisattva: the eleven faces of compassion
buddhi02.lead: Guanyin Bodhisattva is the Chinese name of Avalokiteśvara, the bodhisattva of compassion. In this guided meditation, you meet the eleven-faced form of Guanyin and look at one situation of your own through each face. You move from simply seeing the facts to acting with wisdom.

sections.h2: Who is Guanyin Bodhisattva?
p: Guanyin is the name Chinese Buddhists give to Avalokiteśvara, the great bodhisattva of compassion. It is short for Guanshiyin, the one who perceives the sounds of the world. In other words, a presence that hears every call for help.

In India and Tibet, Avalokiteśvara is usually shown as a man. Over the centuries, Chinese art came to show Guanyin mostly as a woman, often dressed in white. The session speaks of him, following the Indian and Tibetan images. The compassion is the same either way.
Guanyin is one of the most loved bodhisattvas across East Asia. The eleven-faced form is an ancient one, and the session reminds you that each tradition reads those faces in its own way.

sections.h2: What happens during the meditation?
p: You close your eyes, breathe and relax your forehead, your jaw and your shoulders. A white light appears, and within it Avalokiteśvara, one face after another. You don’t need to see all eleven clearly. Petals of light fall slowly, and one settles warm in your hand.
Then you choose a situation you would like to understand better. It becomes the thread of the whole practice.

The first two faces teach you to see only the facts and to listen for the needs beneath the words. The third looks kindly at a past self who was suffering. The next ones bring compassion for someone difficult, patience and a boundary set without hatred.
Then come forgiveness, courage and calm toward everyone. The tenth face widens the circle from your street to the whole Earth. The eleventh is Amitābha, a reminder that compassion needs wisdom.

At the end, the faces merge back into one. You return to your situation and choose the face you could try by tomorrow, with one concrete action. Avalokiteśvara fades into the light, and you come back to your body and the sounds around you.

sections.h2: A Buddhist compassion meditation with clear eyes
p: Compassion here is not about being nice at any cost. The first face starts with facts, the kind a camera could record. Later faces separate understanding from excusing, and helping from rescuing.
This echoes an old Mahayana image. Compassion and wisdom are the two wings of a bird, and a bird cannot fly on one wing.

Kindness also turns inward. The third face looks at a past version of you the way you would look at someone else. The aim is not to approve everything. It is to see a pain without letting it define you.

sections.h2: How should you prepare, and what if a face feels hard?
p: Give yourself a little over twenty quiet minutes. Sit on a chair with your feet flat, or on a cushion with your back upright. Lying down works if you can stay awake. Headphones help you follow the voice through the pauses.

Some faces touch tender places: a time you suffered, a difficult person or a grudge you still carry. You don’t have to go further than feels right. The session even says you may admit that you are not ready to forgive yet.

If your mind wanders, come back to your situation or to the warm petal in your hand. If an emotion rises, breathe with it. This Buddhist guided meditation asks for no belief, so you can meet the figure as an image of kindness.

sections.h2: Two bodhisattva meditations to try next
p: A Tibetan legend says that Tārā was born from the tears of Avalokiteśvara. Her session, “Tārā and the Eight Great Dangers”, walks an ancient road through eight inner fears. For clarity rather than compassion, “Mañjuśrī’s Sword” works with the thoughts that keep looping.
Both belong to Buddhist Meditations, eight guided journeys with the great figures of the Mahayana.

faq: Is Guanyin the same as Avalokiteśvara?

Yes. Guanyin is the Chinese name of Avalokiteśvara, the bodhisattva of compassion. Japan calls the same figure Kannon, and Tibet calls it Chenrezig. The images change from one country to another, but they all point to one quality: a compassion that listens.
Why does Guanyin have eleven faces?

Traditions explain it in different ways. A Tibetan story says the bodhisattva’s head broke apart at the sight of so much suffering. The Buddha Amitābha then rebuilt it with eleven faces. The session offers its own reading: eleven ways to look at one situation, from seeing the facts to acting wisely.
What is a bodhisattva?

In Mahayana Buddhism, a bodhisattva is someone who seeks awakening for the sake of all beings, not only for themselves. Guanyin, Tārā and Maitreya are among the best known. In MeditaDream, each one becomes a guide for exploring a quality, such as compassion or clarity.
Do I need to be Buddhist to meditate with Guanyin?

No. You don’t need any belief or prior knowledge. The figure works as a support for attention and kindness, and the questions fit any life. If you are Buddhist, you may recognize familiar ideas, such as compassion joined with wisdom.
How long is the meditation?

A little over twenty minutes, at a calm pace. It is marked as intermediate and asks many questions in a row, but you don’t have to answer them all. It is a free Buddhist meditation that plays offline once downloaded, with no ads.

buddhi07.seo: Maitreya Buddha Meditation: Meet Who You Are Becoming
buddhi07.desc: Maitreya Buddha, the Buddha expected after Gautama Buddha, guides this 20-minute meditation: climb to his garden and meet the person you are becoming.
buddhi07.h1: Maitreya Buddha’s garden: a guided meditation on the person you are becoming
buddhi07.lead: In Buddhist tradition, Maitreya Buddha is the Buddha still to come. He is expected to teach long after Gautama. This 20-minute guided meditation takes you up an old staircase to his imagined garden. There, one question gives way to another: not what will happen to you, but who you are becoming.

sections.h2: Who is Maitreya Buddha?
p: For now, Maitreya is a bodhisattva, a being on the way to full awakening. Tradition says he will become the next Buddha of our world after Gautama Buddha, the teacher who founded Buddhism. Until then, he waits in a heaven called Tuṣita.
He is one of the few bodhisattvas honored in both Theravada and Mahayana Buddhism. Indian and Tibetan art often shows him seated with both feet on the ground, as if ready to rise.
The session opens with this future in a single sentence, then makes it personal. The garden you visit is imagined, inspired by Maitreya rather than taken from a text.

sections.h2: What do you do during the meditation?
p: You close your eyes and picture a very old staircase, with a gentle light above it. With each step, you set down one worry, not to lose it but to see your life from a little higher.
At the top lies a garden of trees and slow water. A small spring rings one clear note with every drop, and you let your breathing slow with it. Maitreya stands in the distance.

Eleven stops follow. You look at your real habits, at an older self in a still pool and at the decisions that shaped you. Then come two paths, a young tree with three seeds and what others passed on to you.

Later stops show the people who shape your future, an open space with no set path and a house of many doors. On a bench, you name what you might leave behind. A possible future self walks toward you and offers advice for today.
Near the exit, Maitreya asks who you need to become. Three words come, and you keep one as a seed. You walk back down and choose one small act for today.

sections.h2: Why ask who you are becoming?
p: Many of us approach the future with a worry: what is going to happen? The garden turns that worry into a question you can work with. You can’t control the whole future, but you can choose a direction.
Buddhist teaching gives great weight to what we repeat. Small habits of attention and speech slowly shape a person. That is why the first stop looks at an ordinary day, not at great intentions.
The future self you meet is not a destiny. It is one possibility, seen through its way of being rather than its status or possessions.

sections.h2: How should you settle in, and what if no answer comes?
p: Find a quiet place where nobody will need you for a while. Sit upright on a chair or a cushion, or lie down if you can stay awake. Headphones help you follow the voice through the pauses. This 20-minute guided Buddhist meditation is marked as intermediate.

Some questions may bring no answer, and that is fine. The session asks you to listen for the simplest answer, even one that surprises you. If your mind drifts, come back to the stop you are in, or to your breath.
Looking back can bring regret, and looking ahead can bring fear. You don’t have to give anything up right away. At the bench, the session only asks you to name what weighs on you.

sections.h2: Two more journeys with the bodhisattvas
p: “Sudhana’s Journey” — The Teachers Along the Path counts Maitreya among its great encounters. It lasts 30 minutes and teaches you to see one situation through many eyes. For clarity, “Mañjuśrī’s Sword” works with the thoughts that keep looping.
Like this one, each is a guided journey meditation, rich in images and open to anyone curious about Buddhism.

faq: Is Maitreya the Laughing Buddha?

In Chinese tradition, yes. The Laughing Buddha is Budai, a tenth-century monk later seen as a form of Maitreya. His round, smiling statues became the most familiar image of Maitreya in China. Elsewhere, Maitreya is usually shown as a crowned bodhisattva.
When will Maitreya Buddha come?

Buddhist texts place his coming very far in the future, once the teaching of Gautama Buddha has been forgotten. Some traditions speak of an almost unimaginable span of years. The session makes no prediction. It uses this future as an image for the person you are becoming.
What does the name Maitreya mean?

Maitreya comes from maitrī, the Sanskrit word for loving-kindness or friendship. In Pali, he is called Metteyya. The root is mettā, the word behind metta or loving-kindness meditation. The Buddha of the future carries kindness in his very name.
Is this meditation religious?

It draws on a Buddhist figure, but it asks for no belief. Maitreya serves as a guide for looking at your habits, your choices and the qualities you want to grow. Anyone curious about Buddhism, or simply about their own path, can follow it.

buddhi08.seo: Bodhisattva Tara: A Guided Meditation on the Eight Fears
buddhi08.desc: Bodhisattva Tara, much loved in Tibetan Buddhism, walks you past eight inner dangers, from pride to doubt, in a guided meditation of nearly 25 minutes.
buddhi08.h1: Bodhisattva Tara and the eight great fears: a guided journey
buddhi08.lead: Bodhisattva Tara is one of the most loved figures in Tibetan Buddhism, long called upon against eight great fears. In this guided meditation, you walk an ancient road beside Green Tara. Each fear appears as an inner obstacle, from pride to doubt, and at the end you keep one quality to practice.

sections.h2: Who is Bodhisattva Tara?
p: In Sanskrit, her name Tārā means “star.” It is also read as “she who carries across.” Tibetans call her Drölma, the one who liberates. She embodies compassion in action.

A well-known legend says she was born from the tears of Avalokiteśvara, the bodhisattva of compassion. Tibetan tradition praises her in twenty-one forms. Green Tara, the one in this session, is linked to swift help and protection from fear.
She sits with one leg folded in meditation and the other stretched out, ready to step down. The session comes back to that posture at the end, as a picture of knowing when to stay and when to rise.

sections.h2: What are the eight great fears?
p: Tradition lists eight dangers from which Tara protects those who call on her. Teachers often read them as eight inner obstacles.

The lion stands for pride, the wild elephant for ignorance and fire for anger. The serpent stands for jealousy, the thieves for wrong views and the prison for greed. The flood stands for attachment and the demons for doubt.
The session adds a hidden ninth obstacle of its own: the fear of change. It can hold you back even when you already know what to do.

sections.h2: How does the journey with Tara unfold?
p: You close your eyes, breathe slowly and feel your body supported. An ancient road crosses plains, forests and mountains. Green Tara appears, and you walk beside her while a wind horse made of cloud and light crosses the sky.

Then each danger blocks the road in turn and raises a few honest questions. Before the lion, you ask what you are defending when you need to be right. In the fire, you ask what your anger is trying to protect. With the serpent, envy becomes a clue to what you want.

In the prison, Tara points to a handle on the door. At sunrise, you look back at the dangers as eight ways of briefly losing your freedom. You choose the one most present in your life, a quality that answers it and one action.
Tara then walks away along the road, and you don’t need to follow her. You keep three words: obstacle, quality, action.

sections.h2: Do you need to know about Tibetan Buddhism?
p: No. The session is not a traditional ritual, and it asks for no belief. It is a guided journey meditation inspired by Tara, with questions anyone can use.
It suits the moments when a fear or a habit keeps deciding for you. Think of a choice you keep postponing, a conflict that lingers or a jealousy you would rather not admit.

Set aside a little under twenty-five minutes. Sit upright on a chair or a cushion, or lie down if you can stay awake. Headphones help you follow the voice through the pauses. This Buddhist guided meditation is marked as intermediate.

sections.h2: What if one danger hits close to home?
p: Some dangers will feel distant and others very personal. You don’t have to answer every question. Stay longer with the one that speaks to you, and let the others pass like the rest of the road.

If anger or envy rises, notice where you feel it in your body, as the session invites you to. Then come back to your breath and to Tara walking beside you. If your mind wanders, return to the road and the next step.
To go further, “The Eleven Faces of Avalokiteśvara” is a natural next step, since legend links Tara to his tears. To keep working with fear, “Mañjuśrī’s Lion” goes down into the valley of old fears.

faq: Is Tara a bodhisattva or a Buddha?

Both views exist. In much of Mahayana Buddhism, Tara is a bodhisattva devoted to helping all beings. Tibetan Buddhism often goes further and honors her as a fully awakened Buddha in female form. In the session, you simply meet her as a calm guide on the road.
What is the difference between Green Tara and White Tara?

Green Tara is linked to swift, active compassion and protection from fear, which is why she leads this session. White Tara is linked to long life and serene compassion. Both belong to the twenty-one forms of Tara praised in Tibetan tradition.
Does the session use the Tara mantra?

No. Her best-known mantra, om tare tuttare ture soha, is not chanted here. The session is a guided journey of images and questions. If you already recite the mantra, you can keep it as a practice of your own, before or after.
Do I need to believe in Tara?
No. You can see Tara as a figure of the Tibetan tradition, as an inner image or simply as a guide for attention. The questions about pride, anger or doubt apply to anyone, whatever they believe.

cons02.seo: Chakra Sleep Meditation: The Seven Chakras at Bedtime
cons02.desc: Chakra sleep meditation for bedtime: 18 minutes lying down, through the seven chakras, with colors, quiet phrases and long pauses. Free, with no ads.
cons02.h1: Chakra sleep meditation: a slow evening journey from root to crown
cons02.lead: This chakra sleep meditation, called “Chakra Reset” in the app, guides you through the seven chakras in 18 slow minutes. You climb from the base of the spine to the top of the head. Each center gets a color, a few silent phrases and a long pause. Lie down and let the day go.

sections.h2: What happens in this chakra sleep meditation?
p: You begin by relaxing your body, your shoulders and your jaw. Any task that comes back to mind is put away for tomorrow. After three slow breaths, the voice sets the aim for the evening: a gentle visit to each chakra, with nothing to force.
You feel the whole length of your spine, then start at its base. A deep red light glows there like embers. You feel the weight of your hips and legs and picture roots beneath you.

Then the journey climbs. Orange light flows like slow water below the navel. Golden yellow shines under the ribs and spreads into your arms and hands. At the heart, green light makes room for peace, and a unicorn comes to rest its head on your shoulder.

Blue light cools the throat, and the words you didn’t say today can rest. Indigo settles between the eyebrows while thoughts drift by like clouds. Last, a violet-white light flows down from the top of the head through every center.

At each center, you repeat a few short phrases silently, such as “I am safe.” The seven colors then line up into one stream of light. The session ends with a soft return: you move your fingers and shoulders, then open your eyes.

sections.h2: The seven chakras and their colors
p: Chakra means “wheel” in Sanskrit. The yoga traditions of India describe chakras as centers of subtle energy along the spine. The seven-chakra map with rainbow colors that most people know became popular in the twentieth century.

Here, red sits at the base of the spine, orange below the navel and yellow under the ribs. Green belongs to the heart, blue to the throat and indigo to the forehead. The crown receives a violet-white light.
You don’t need to believe in chakras to use them tonight. They work as seven resting points for your attention, climbing slowly from the ground to the sky.

sections.h2: How to use it as a night meditation
p: Lie on your back in bed with the lights low. A pillow under your knees can ease your lower back. Put your phone face down beside you.

Once the session is downloaded, switch to airplane mode and it still plays. Headphones are optional. Soft earbuds help if someone sleeps beside you, and a speaker at low volume works when you are alone.
It fits easily into a sleep routine: lights off, phone down, session on. The pace is slow and the pauses are long, so it also works simply as relaxation for sleep.

sections.h2: What if you feel nothing, or fall asleep?
p: You may not see any color or feel any warmth. That is fine. The session asks only for your attention, and a single place in the body is enough to rest it on.
If you fall asleep before the end, nothing is lost. The colors and the phrases do not need to be followed to the last one.

At the heart, the session invites you to let old emotional pain soften. If an emotion rises, let it be there and come back to the weight of your body on the bed. If a phrase doesn’t feel true tonight, just listen to it without forcing yourself to agree.

sections.h2: Which guided meditation for sleep comes next?
p: If you prefer a session with no return at the end, try “Drifting into Sleep”. It lasts 16 minutes and lets sleep come at its own pace. To learn where each chakra sits before you picture it, try “Recognizing the Seven Chakras”, a 28-minute body map.
Both are in Body, Calm & Sleep. Like every session in MeditaDream, they are free and play offline once downloaded.

faq: Can I do this chakra meditation and sleep right after?

Yes. Falling asleep before the end is fine. If you are still awake at the close, the voice invites you to move your fingers and open your eyes. You can then turn off the light, stay lying down and let the calm carry on.
Do I need to believe in chakras?

No. You can see the chakras as a spiritual map from India or simply as seven points of attention along the body. Either way, the session works the same: one place, one color and a few quiet phrases at a time.
Can I do it sitting up?
Yes. Sitting against a pillow works if you want to stay awake through all seven chakras. Lying on your back suits bedtime better, when you are happy to drift off before the end.
Is “Chakra Reset” free?
Yes. MeditaDream is free, with no ads and no account. Download the session once and it plays offline, so your phone can stay in airplane mode all night. No session asks for a subscription.

corps01.seo: Breathing Exercises for Sleep: A Gentle 13-Minute Practice
corps01.desc: Breathing exercises for sleep you can do in bed: a 13-minute guided relaxation for sleep that follows each breath into your ribs, back and pelvis.
corps01.h1: Breathing exercises for sleep: let the whole body breathe
corps01.lead: These breathing exercises for sleep use no breath counts and no breath holding. For 13 minutes, lying in bed or sitting, you notice how far each breath travels: into the ribs, the back, even the pelvis. It is a quiet way to slow down before the night.

sections.h2: Step by step: what you do in these breathing exercises for sleep
p: You start by settling in and simply watching your breath as it is, without trying to deepen it. Then your attention begins to travel. It rests on the center of the chest, then moves to the sides, where the ribs spread a little on each inhale, like a fan opening. It goes down to the belly, which you let move on its own, and then to the direction most of us forget: the back, between and below the shoulder blades.

Next comes an image: your torso as a large vase that opens slightly on every in-breath and settles on every out-breath. Your attention sinks to the pelvis, where each breath arrives like a soft ripple on a pond. You even swap the words in your head, from breathing with your lungs to a new thought: “My whole body is taking part in this breath.”

Later, you look for the small turning point between inhale and exhale, without holding anything, and play with the feeling of breathing through the whole surface of the body. At the end, the breath becomes natural again and you come back to the points of contact. The excerpt above covers the opening minutes.

sections.h2: What makes a breathing exercise good for sleep?
p: A good breathing exercise for the night is slow, easy and comfortable to do in bed. Some well-known methods give the mind a task: box breathing and 4-7-8 breathing rely on counts and pauses, while diaphragmatic breathing teaches you to breathe low into the belly on purpose.

This session belongs to the gentlest family. You never count your breaths, hold them or push them. The belly moves by itself, and your attention widens to the ribs and the back, so the breath can feel three-dimensional instead of stuck in the chest. It draws on an old idea from early Buddhism: attention to the breath can widen to the whole body. Think of it as a relaxation meditation, guided by your own breathing rather than by a story.

sections.h2: Relaxation for sleep: when to do it and how to set up
p: Do it in bed, lights low, once you are ready to let the day go. Lying on your back helps you feel the back and pelvis against the mattress, which the session explores in detail, but sitting against a pillow works too. Headphones are optional. Download the session first: it then plays offline, so your phone can stay in airplane mode, face down on the nightstand.

As guided relaxation for sleep, it is a first step rather than a sleep session. It ends by inviting you to feel your points of contact and open your eyes, so it does not carry you all the way into sleep. You can then turn off the light and settle in, or play a session made to end without a wake-up.

sections.h2: What if your mind wanders or the breath feels forced?
p: Thoughts will come. Let them pass and return to the simple question the session gives you: where is this breath moving in my body right now? The answer is allowed to change with every breath.

Some areas, often the back or the pelvis, may barely register. Don’t force them; simply invite them in with your attention. If the breath starts to feel controlled, stop guiding it and let it run by itself for a few rounds. And if you drift off before the end, that is perfectly fine at bedtime.

sections.h2: Fitting it into your sleep routine
p: This practice fits well in the middle of a sleep routine: screens off, these 13 minutes of breathing, then lights out. For a longer evening, follow it with “Sleep Journey”, a 27-minute session that lets you slide toward sleep with no wake-up at the end. If you enjoy working with the breath, “The Luminous Breath”, also 13 minutes, pairs each in-breath with an image of light moving down from the belly to the legs.

faq: Can breathing exercises help you fall asleep?

Not directly: no exercise can switch sleep on. A slow breathing practice gives your mind one quiet thing to follow instead of replaying the day. This one uses no breath counts and no effort, which makes it easy to do in bed with the lights off.
Is this the 4-7-8 breathing method?

No. The 4-7-8 method uses a fixed count and a held breath. This session never counts your breaths and never asks you to hold them: you notice the breath as it is and let your attention follow it into the ribs, the back and the pelvis.
Is it better to lie down or sit up?

Lying on your back suits bedtime best: the contact with the bed makes small movements in the back and pelvis easier to feel. Sit up against a pillow if you tend to fall asleep early and want to follow the whole practice.
Is the session free?

Yes. “Breathing with the Whole Body” is part of MeditaDream, a free meditation app with 144 guided meditations, no ads and no account. Once downloaded, the session plays offline, even in airplane mode.

reves02.seo: Deep Sleep Meditation: 27 Minutes, No Wake-Up at the End
reves02.desc: Deep sleep meditation for bedtime: a 27-minute night meditation that softens the body, walks you through a garden at dusk and ends without waking you.
reves02.h1: Deep sleep meditation: a slow journey into sleep
reves02.lead: This deep sleep meditation is made for the moment you lie down for the night. For 27 minutes, a slow voice guides you through your body, then into a quiet garden at dusk, until the images blur. There is nothing to remember, and no wake-up at the end.

sections.h2: What happens during this deep sleep meditation
p: You begin in the position you sleep in and let the bed take your weight. The first part stays with the body. You feel where it touches the mattress, then tense your toes and legs very gently and let go, just enough to notice the difference. The release then moves upward, from the hips and belly to the jaw and the small muscles around the eyes. The excerpt above covers this part.

Then the journey begins. You step through a small wooden gate into an old walled garden just after sunset. You walk a mossy path and sit on a bench still warm from the day, leaving your worries behind the wall. A shooting star crosses the sky, then fireflies appear and vanish, the way attention comes and goes.

Further on, you reach a dark pool. A thought becomes a ripple that fades if you leave the water alone. From there, the story loosens on purpose: images drift and blend, a calm sea at night comes and goes, and the voice tells you that you no longer need to follow it. The session ends without calling you back.

sections.h2: Can a meditation give you deep sleep?
p: Not on command; no recording can. Deep sleep arrives on its own. What people usually mean by a deep sleep meditation is a session made for bedtime that leads you toward sleep instead of keeping you alert, and ideally does not wake you at the end.

“Sleep Journey” is built that way. It starts with the body, because heaviness is easy to notice. It moves into a gentle story, because images can hold attention more softly than worries. Then it lets the story fall apart, since following a plot is something we do awake. By the end, nothing is asked of you.

sections.h2: A night meditation in bed: how to set up
p: Get into bed and settle into your usual sleeping position; the voice even asks you to stop looking for the perfect one. Lower the lights and put your phone face down. A speaker at low volume works as well as headphones, and may be more comfortable if you sleep on your side.

Download the session beforehand so it plays offline in airplane mode. At 27 minutes, this guided meditation for sleep takes its time. On evenings when you only want a short wind-down, a shorter session will suit you better.

sections.h2: What if you are still awake, or your mind keeps talking?
p: It happens, and the session expects it. When a thought arrives, you watch it cross the pool like a ripple instead of pushing it away. Losing track is welcome here: you can let a sentence slip by, then several, without going back.

If you are still awake at the end, that is fine too. As the voice puts it, “Whether you are already asleep or not, either way is fine.” Stay where you are, eyes closed, and let the silence go on. Odd sensations, like a hand that feels far away, are a common part of drifting off, and you don’t need to fix them.

sections.h2: Meditation and sleep: what to try next
p: For a shorter evening, “Drifting into Sleep” takes 16 minutes and also ends without a wake-up. If your body still feels tense when you get into bed, start with “Breathing with the Whole Body”, a 13-minute breathing practice, then let “Sleep Journey” take over. Both are in the Body, Calm & Sleep category.

faq: What is yoga nidra, and is this the same?

Yoga nidra is a guided practice, usually done lying down, that invites you to stay aware on the edge of sleep. “Sleep Journey” shares its slow attention to the body but goes the other way: it lets sleep come and never calls you back.
Can I listen to it every night?

Yes. It is designed for bedtime and can become part of every evening. If it starts to feel too familiar, alternate it with “Drifting into Sleep”, a shorter guided meditation for deep sleep that also ends without waking you.
Why does the story stop making sense?

On purpose. Following a plot keeps part of the mind awake, so after the pool the images are free to drift and blend. If a different image appears on its own, the voice invites you to follow it rather than return to the garden.
Is this guided meditation for sleep and relaxation free?
Yes. “Sleep Journey” is part of MeditaDream, a free meditation app with 144 guided meditations, no ads and no account. Once downloaded, it plays offline, so nothing interrupts you during the night.

appren02.seo: Breathing Meditation: Steady Your Attention in 13 Minutes
appren02.desc: Breathing meditation, guided step by step: choose one anchor, count your out-breaths up to five and come back each time the mind wanders. 13 minutes.
appren02.h1: Guided breathing meditation: find your thread again
appren02.lead: Breathing meditation means resting your attention on the breath and coming back each time it drifts. This 13-minute session for beginners teaches exactly that: one anchor, a simple count and a kind way to return. You don’t need to breathe perfectly. You only need to notice.

sections.h2: How to do this breathing meditation, step by step
p: You sit in a stable position, back straight but not stiff, eyes closed. First, you let the breath be natural and look for the place where it is easiest to feel: the nostrils, the chest or the belly. You choose one, and that spot becomes your anchor for the whole session.

Then you follow each breath from its very start to its end. Soon the mind wanders, and that is expected. The voice compares the breath to Ariadne’s thread in the labyrinth: you get lost in a corridor, realize it and return. You also learn to catch attention as it starts to blur, which often happens gradually. The excerpt above takes you this far.

Next comes counting. You count each exhalation, placing the number at the very end of the out-breath, up to five, then start again at one. Reaching eight or twelve simply shows you drifted. After that, you drop the count and follow whole breaths with their small turning points. You then widen your awareness, keeping the breath in the foreground while the body and sounds stay in the background. You finish by following three breaths very closely, then notice how your mind feels now.

sections.h2: Why breath counting is one of the oldest mindfulness exercises
p: Breath counting appears in many contemplative traditions, from early Buddhist manuals to Zen, where some people practice with the breath for years. Its value is that it makes the mind’s habits visible. Within a minute, you may see impatience, a daydream or plain boredom come and go.

That is the link between meditation and mindfulness: you are not trying to empty your mind, you are training the return. If you have wondered how to do mindfulness meditation, this is its simplest form: one anchor and many returns. The count makes each return visible. Losing count is not a failure; realizing you lost it is the moment the practice happens.

sections.h2: Is breathing meditation good for beginners?
p: Yes. The session is marked beginner and explains each step as it goes, so it works as a first real practice. It also suits experienced meditators who want to rebuild a steady base. Think of it as guided mindfulness in its most basic form.

Sit on a chair or a cushion with your back upright and relaxed. You can lie down, but you may doze off more easily. Choose a quiet place and a moment when you feel awake, such as the morning or a break in your day. Headphones help with the quiet instructions but are optional, and the session plays offline once downloaded.

sections.h2: What if your mind keeps wandering?
p: Then the practice is doing its job. Stability, in this session, is not the absence of distraction but the habit of coming back a little sooner each time. When you notice you have drifted, greet that moment with a small inner smile rather than a reproach, and come back to the physical feeling of the air, not to the idea of breathing.

The voice offers a gentle image for this: a puppy learning to stay close. Each time it wanders off, you simply call it back, without scolding. Treat impatience or boredom the same way. If you catch yourself controlling the breath, soften the belly and let the breath find its own rhythm again.

sections.h2: After breathing meditation: what comes next
p: Once the breath feels like a reliable anchor, try “Observing Thoughts” — Watching the Trains Go by. In 15 minutes, it uses the breath as a base to watch thoughts arrive, name them and let them go. When you feel ready for more silence, “Your First Silent Meditation” lasts five minutes and leaves real space between the instructions. Both are in the Learning Basics category.

faq: How do I learn to meditate if my mind never stops?

Start with the breath and expect the mind to wander. The skill is not stopping thoughts but noticing that you have drifted and coming back. A count from one to five, like the one in this session, makes each return easy to spot. Short, regular sessions help more than long, rare ones.
Should I breathe deeply during breathing meditation?

No. You leave the breath natural and simply feel it. If you catch yourself slowing it down or deepening it, let the belly soften and the breath return to its own pace. The breath is a meeting point for your attention, not something to perfect.
Where should I focus: nose, chest or belly?

Wherever the breath is easiest to feel for you today. At the nostrils, notice the slightly cool air coming in. At the chest, the rise and fall. At the belly, the gentle movement out and back. Pick one spot and keep it for the whole session.
What is mindfulness meditation, compared with breathing meditation?

Mindfulness meditation is the broad practice of noticing what happens, moment by moment, without judging it. Breathing meditation is its most common starting point: the breath is always there, easy to feel, and it shows clearly when attention drifts away.
