chi02.seo: Microcosmic Orbit Meditation: A Guided 22-Minute Practice
chi02.desc: Microcosmic orbit meditation, step by step: a 22-minute seated practice that moves your attention up the back and down the front, with qigong breathing.
chi02.h1: Microcosmic orbit meditation: the Small Circulation, step by step
chi02.lead: Microcosmic orbit meditation follows a loop through the body: from the lower belly down to the pelvis, up the back to the crown, then down the front. In this 22-minute session, you trace it with your attention, helped by a small glowing pearl. Feeling energy is not required.

sections.h2: What you do in this microcosmic orbit meditation
p: You sit upright with your hands on your lower belly and start by feeling your whole body on the seat. Your attention then settles just below the navel, where you picture a small warm point. The first lap is slow and precise. You go down to the base of the pelvis, then climb the back region by region, all the way to the crown. You come down the front, through the face, throat and chest, and return to the belly. The excerpt above covers most of this first lap.

Then the path becomes smoother. A small glowing pearl travels the loop, which helps keep the route precise, and you learn to slow down where the back feels vague. You split the circuit into three parts, practice each one, then join them. Later, if it feels comfortable, you add the breath.

Toward the end, you let the pearl fade, then follow the loop without it, so that only attention moves. You give the loop depth by feeling the back behind the chest. Finally, the pearl stops in the lower belly, under your hands, and you compare your body with how it felt at the start.

sections.h2: What is the microcosmic orbit?
p: The microcosmic orbit, known in Taoism as the Small Circulation, is a classic of Chinese inner practice. In the traditional description, qi rises along a channel that follows the spine and comes down another along the front of the body, forming one closed loop. Many schools teach it as a seated chi kung meditation, often with the tip of the tongue resting on the palate to join the two paths. This session does not ask for that.

It also stays modest. From the first minutes, it presents the loop mainly as a precise route for your attention, and says the practice counts even if you feel no current at all. Warmth or tingling may appear, or nothing in particular. The aim is steady attention and a clearer sense of your own body.

sections.h2: Can beginners practice the microcosmic orbit?
p: Yes, with a little patience. The session is marked intermediate. The route has many stages and asks for 22 minutes of precise attention, but every step is explained. If you are looking for qigong meditation for beginners, “Warming the Hands” is a gentler place to start.

Sit on a chair or a cushion with your back naturally upright, not rigid. A quiet room is enough; you don’t need space to move. Pick a time when you feel alert, since this is attention work rather than a practice for falling asleep. Headphones help you follow the small details of the route, but they are optional. It is a free qigong practice that plays offline once downloaded.

sections.h2: Adding qigong breathing, and what you may feel
p: Midway, the session invites you to link the pearl to your breathing: it rises along the back as you inhale and comes down the front as you exhale. This is a simple form of qigong breathing. If your in-breath ends before the crown, the movement just continues. If the rhythm feels long or uncomfortable, you drop it and keep following the loop on its own.

Everyone feels this practice differently. You may notice warmth in the back, a tingling or nothing special. Don’t chase a sensation: if you catch yourself waiting for one, come back to the area itself. If you lose your place, pick up again from the last area you felt, and if a region stays vague, slow down there and simply locate it.

sections.h2: Guided qigong meditation: what to try next
p: If the loop felt hard to hold, begin with “Warming the Hands”, 20 minutes spent feeling an imaginary ball between your palms. If you enjoyed this session and want to practice standing, “The Still Tree” brings the same unhurried attention into a rooted posture, in 23 minutes. Both are in the Sensations & Qigong category.

faq: Which way does the microcosmic orbit flow?

In this session, attention goes down from the lower belly to the base of the pelvis, up along the back to the crown, then down the front of the body to the belly. Up the back and down the front is the direction most commonly taught.
Do I need to feel energy for it to work?

No. The session treats the loop first as a precise route for your attention. Some people notice warmth or tingling, others very little, and both are fine. If you catch yourself waiting for something to happen, return to the spot you are on and keep following the path.
What is qigong, in a few words?

Qigong is a family of Chinese practices that bring posture, breath and attention together, whether you stand still, sit or move slowly. The microcosmic orbit belongs to its seated, meditative side, with roots in Taoist inner practice.
What is the difference between the microcosmic and macrocosmic orbit?

The microcosmic orbit is the small loop along the back and the front of the torso and head. The macrocosmic orbit, usually taught later, extends the circuit through the arms and legs. This session stays with the small loop from start to finish.

chi03.seo: Tree Meditation: Guided Standing Qigong in 23 Minutes
chi03.desc: Tree meditation from qigong: stand for 23 minutes, feet rooted and arms around an imaginary ball, then finish with a few slow steps. Guided and free.
chi03.h1: Tree meditation: stand still, rooted like a tree
chi03.lead: This tree meditation comes from qigong standing practice: you stand still, feet rooted, arms rounded as if holding a large ball. For 23 minutes, the voice helps you find your balance, release unneeded tension and let your body hold the posture without strain. You finish with a few slow steps.

sections.h2: What you do in this tree meditation, step by step
p: You stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart and your knees slightly bent, while the crown of your head rises gently. Before anything else, you explore your balance: tiny shifts forward and back, then side to side, then small circles in both directions, until you find the middle.

Then the image of the tree arrives, with roots under your feet and a trunk that runs up through your legs and pelvis. You check each part of your legs. The excerpt above ends as your arms rise slowly in front of you, as if holding a large ball at chest height, elbows low and shoulders loose.

The rest of this guided tree meditation refines the posture. Roots grow beneath each foot. Each in-breath lengthens the spine, each out-breath settles your weight. Your arms become branches, and you release tension down to the thumbs and little fingers. You notice the tiny movements that keep you balanced, feel diagonal links between elbows and knees, and imagine a light breeze that sways you a few millimeters. Finally, the ball grows lighter, your arms come down slowly, and you take a few slow steps before walking normally.

sections.h2: What is a tree meditation?
p: The phrase covers two related ideas. The first is an image: you picture yourself as a tree, rooted in the ground with open branches, to feel steadier. The second is a classic of Chinese standing practice, zhan zhuang, usually translated as “standing like a post” and often called “standing like a tree.” In this chi kung meditation, you hold one simple posture and let attention do the work.

“The Still Tree” brings the two together. Roots, trunk and branches guide your attention, while the posture itself, arms around an imaginary ball, comes from standing qigong. It is also a grounding exercise in the most literal sense: your attention keeps returning to your feet, your legs and the weight settling down.

sections.h2: Is the tree a good beginner meditation?
p: Yes, if you can stand comfortably for about twenty minutes. It is marked intermediate, yet the instructions themselves are simple, and the voice explains every detail.

Practice in a quiet room with a little space around you, since the session ends with a few steps. Flat shoes or bare feet on a stable floor work best. Your eyes can stay open on a point in front of you or closed, as you prefer. Morning or a break in the day suits this alert practice better than bedtime. Headphones are optional.

sections.h2: What if your arms or shoulders get tired?
p: They may, especially at first, and the session plans for it. Lower your elbows a little, relax your wrists and let your chest soften, then return to the shape. Imagining that the ball supports your forearms from within can make the posture feel lighter. If anything hurts sharply, lower your arms or stop, as the session itself advises.

Small sways are part of the practice: even a tree that looks still keeps moving a little, and so does a standing body. If your mind wanders, come back to the contact of your feet with the ground. When your arms come down, notice what changes, such as warmth or heaviness in the hands, without interpreting it.

sections.h2: After the tree: more guided qigong meditation
p: To move from stillness into motion, “The Dance of Qi” — Qigong in Motion offers 25 minutes of slow movement in which feet, hands and torso answer one another. If you would rather sit, “The Small Circulation” guides your attention along a loop up the back and down the front, in 22 minutes. Both are in the Sensations & Qigong category.

faq: Is it the same as tree pose in yoga?

No. In yoga’s tree pose, you balance on one leg. In this tree meditation, both feet stay on the ground, knees soft, and the arms are rounded in front of the chest. The tree is an image for rootedness here, not a balancing challenge.
How long should I hold the standing posture?

There is no fixed rule. In the session, your arms stay raised for most of the 23 minutes, and you can lower them whenever you need to. If you practice on your own later, a few minutes is a good start: comfort matters more than duration.
Should my eyes be open or closed?

Either works. With eyes open, rest your gaze on one point in front of you, since a steady gaze can help your balance. With eyes closed, simply keep your head facing the same way. If you feel unsteady, open them.
Is this a free qigong session?
Yes. “The Still Tree” is part of MeditaDream, a free meditation app with no ads, no subscription and no account. Once downloaded, it plays offline, so you can practice at home or outdoors.

lieux01.seo: Bodhi Tree Meditation: A 17-Minute Dawn Journey to Bodh Gaya
lieux01.desc: Bodhi tree meditation at dawn: a 17-minute guided journey beneath the tree linked to the Buddha’s enlightenment. Sit or lie down. Free, plays offline.
lieux01.h1: Bodhi tree meditation: dawn beneath the tree of awakening
lieux01.lead: This bodhi tree meditation takes you, in imagination, to dawn on the plains of Bihar, where Buddhist tradition places the Buddha’s awakening. For 17 minutes, you walk to the great tree, watch its leaves catch the first light and sit among its roots. After that, you can simply stay.

sections.h2: What happens in this bodhi tree meditation
p: After a moment to settle, you find yourself walking barefoot on cool earth before sunrise. A single bell rings far away. Out of the dim plain, one tree stands out, wider and older than the rest: the Bodhi tree. Its heart-shaped leaves tremble until the first ray of sun turns them gold, one by one. You step under its branches and sit down, which is where the excerpt above ends.

With the trunk at your back, the voice recalls the story of the place and the pilgrims who came after the Buddha. Then it lets them all fade, until only you, the tree and the dawn remain. You feel your pelvis settle like a root. A breeze runs through the leaves, then silence returns. A leaf falls, turns and lands. You look at the patches of sky between the branches, and treat passing thoughts the same way, noticing the space they leave.

Later, pilgrims pass in the distance and the first sunlight warms one side of your face. Near the end, a small oil lamp burns beside a stone, a picture of steady attention. Then the voice leaves the place open: you can watch one leaf, listen to the birds or just sit, for as long as you wish.

sections.h2: The Bodhi tree and the Buddha’s enlightenment
p: The Bodhi tree is a sacred fig that grows at Bodh Gaya, in the Indian state of Bihar. According to Buddhist tradition, Siddhartha Gautama sat beneath it some 2,500 years ago and reached awakening, becoming the Buddha. Bodhi means “awakening” in Pali and Sanskrit. The tree that grows there today, beside the Mahabodhi Temple, is described as a descendant of the original, and the site is one of the Buddha’s great sacred places.

A bodhi tree meditation uses this setting as a support for attention. The session does not ask you to relive the Buddha’s enlightenment or to adopt a belief. It lets the story give the place depth, then leaves you alone with the tree. Countless pilgrims travel to this spot, one of the most revered sacred sites of Buddhism.

sections.h2: A guided morning meditation, or a pause at any hour
p: Because the whole journey unfolds at sunrise, it makes a natural guided morning meditation, but it suits any quiet moment. Sit on a chair or a cushion, or lie down if you prefer; the session only asks for a steady position and relaxed shoulders. Lying down can invite sleep, so sit up if you want to stay with the images until the end.

Headphones are optional but help you catch the quiet details. Once downloaded, the session plays offline. You don’t need to be Buddhist, or to have seen the place, to follow it: the voice describes the light, the leaves and the sounds.

sections.h2: What if thoughts keep coming?
p: Let them come. The session gives you a simple tool: look at the patches of blue sky between the branches, not at the leaves themselves, and when a thought passes, notice the space it leaves behind. Nothing has to be pushed away.

Images may also stay vague, especially if you have never seen the place. That is fine: the cool shade or a single golden leaf is enough. If the story or the stillness stirs an emotion, stay with your breath and the feeling of the ground beneath you. The last part is open, so you can end whenever you like.

sections.h2: From Buddhist sacred spaces to a Taoist sanctuary
p: In the same Sacred Places category, “The Ancient Pagoda Among the Lotuses” takes 15 minutes. It walks you through a fine rain in a Japanese valley to an old pagoda, a Buddhist temple at the heart of a lotus pond. “The Taoist Sanctuary in the Mountains” opens at dawn above a sea of clouds, also in 15 minutes. Each one uses a place to steady your attention, at the same unhurried pace.

faq: Do I need to be Buddhist to do a bodhi tree meditation?

No. The session uses the setting and its story as a support for attention, without asking for any belief. You walk, sit and look. People of any background can follow it, with respect for what the place means to Buddhists.
What kind of tree is the Bodhi tree?

It is a sacred fig, Ficus religiosa, also called pipal or peepal in India. Its heart-shaped leaves end in a long, thin tip that trembles in the slightest breeze, a detail the session lingers on as the first light reaches them.
When is Bodhi Day?

Many Mahayana communities, especially in Japan, mark the Buddha’s awakening on December 8, known as Bodhi Day or Rohatsu. Theravada traditions celebrate it at Vesak, a full-moon festival usually held in May. This meditation can be a quiet way to mark either date.
Can I stay longer at the end?

Yes. The last part is left open on purpose: the voice invites you to watch a leaf, listen to the birds or simply sit, and to stay as long as you wish. When the session ends, you can remain in silence a little longer.

cons06.seo: Compassion Meditation: A 7-Minute Practice in Five Circles
cons06.desc: Compassion meditation in 7 minutes: offer kind wishes to yourself, then to others in widening circles, up to all beings. A gentle start for inner compassion.
cons06.h1: Compassion meditation: kindness in five widening circles
cons06.lead: This compassion meditation takes just 7 minutes. You silently offer a few simple wishes, first to yourself, then to people in widening circles, from someone you love to someone you find difficult, and finally to all beings. Wishing someone well never means excusing what they did.

sections.h2: How this compassion meditation unfolds
p: You sit with your spine tall and relaxed and take three full, slow breaths to arrive. The voice explains that the practice is called metta, or loving-kindness, and that kindness will travel through five circles, beginning with you.

First, you picture yourself in a mirror and look at yourself kindly while silently repeating four short wishes at the pace of your breath, beginning with “May I be safe.” Next comes someone dear to you, a person or even a pet. Then a neutral person you barely know, like a neighbor or a stranger on your commute, whose day holds hopes and worries just like yours. Then someone mildly difficult, seen as a person who struggles too. The excerpt above takes you to this point.

Finally, the circle opens to all beings, near and far. You picture them as small lights across the Earth, linked by the roots of a great tree of light, with yourself among them. You bring the warmth back to yourself, thank your heart and open your eyes.

sections.h2: Compassion meditation or loving-kindness: what is the difference?
p: In Buddhist teaching, the two are close cousins. Loving-kindness, called metta in Pali, is the wish that beings be happy and at peace. Compassion, karuna, is the wish that they be free from suffering. Teachers often practice them together, and in everyday English, compassion meditation can simply mean a metta practice like this one.

This session is a short, guided loving-kindness meditation in the classic metta form, with its widening circles and repeated phrases. Its most compassionate step comes with the difficult person, whom you see as someone who struggles too. Nothing here forces a feeling: you repeat an intention, and inner compassion is something you practice, not something you must feel on cue.

sections.h2: When to practice compassion meditation, and how to sit
p: Seven minutes fits almost anywhere: in the morning before the day takes over, after a tense conversation or in the evening. Sit comfortably with your back tall but relaxed. You can lie down if you prefer, as long as you stay awake enough to picture each person. Headphones are optional.

If you are new to it, choose an easy person for the second circle and someone only mildly irritating for the fourth, never the person who hurt you most. The same people can come back day after day; there is no need to change them each time.

sections.h2: What if it feels hard, or nothing happens?
p: Both are common. Wishing yourself well can feel awkward, and the difficult person may bring up irritation instead of warmth. The session offers a way out: if the difficult person feels like too much, return to your own circle for a moment, then go on when you are ready.

If you feel nothing, that is fine too. The words carry the intention, and warmth may come later, or not today. If an emotion rises, such as sadness or tenderness, let it be there and keep breathing at your own pace. For heavier feelings, “Welcoming a Difficult Emotion”, in the same category, gives them more room.

sections.h2: After compassion meditation: what to try next
p: To go deeper into the first circle, “Developing Self-love” invites you to find something real in yourself, like perseverance or curiosity, and give it a little love, in 15 minutes. “Opening Your Heart to Love”, also 15 minutes, explores the chest from front and back and meets the feeling of not deserving without arguing with it. Both are gentle self-compassion exercises, done at your own pace.

faq: What phrases do you repeat in compassion meditation?

In this session, you repeat four short wishes, from safety to peace, slowly and in rhythm with your breath. They are the classic wishes of metta loving-kindness practice, said for yourself first, then for each circle. Outside the session, you can adapt the words, as long as they feel sincere to you.
Do I have to forgive the difficult person?

No. Wishing someone safety and peace does not mean approving of what they did or keeping them close. The session says so clearly: nothing is excused. Start with someone mildly annoying rather than someone who hurt you deeply, and come back to yourself if it feels like too much.
Is 7 minutes enough?

Yes, for a daily practice. Seven minutes lets you go through all five circles without rushing, and short, regular sessions often help more than long, rare ones. When you want more time, follow it with a longer session from the Emotional Growth category.
Is this a self-compassion meditation?

Partly. The first and last circles are turned toward you, which is the heart of self-compassion. Most of the practice, though, widens toward others. For a self-compassion meditation centered on you, try “Developing Self-love”, a 15-minute session in the same category.

croiss03.seo: Gratitude Meditation: A Guided Walk Through Your Day
croiss03.desc: Gratitude meditation in 14 minutes: walk through a small museum of your day, one ordinary moment per room, then keep just one. Free, no ads, no account.
croiss03.h1: A guided gratitude meditation through the small museum of your day
croiss03.lead: A gratitude meditation is a few quiet minutes spent noticing what already went right, without pretending everything is fine. In “Daily Gratitude”, you walk through a small imaginary museum of your day. Each room holds an ordinary moment, like a first sip, a familiar sound or a door held open.

sections.h2: What is a gratitude meditation?
p: A gratitude meditation is a guided practice where you bring back small good moments and stay with them a little longer than usual. You don’t list what you should be thankful for. You relive one moment with your senses: a taste, a sound, a face.
The session is clear about one thing: “Gratitude, here, doesn’t require you to be happy.” Hard things stay what they are. You simply look, for a moment, at what usually goes unnoticed.

Meditation and gratitude fit well together. Meditation slows your attention down, and gratitude gives it something kind to rest on. Practicing gratitude through a guided meditation also feels different from writing a list: you don’t search for words, you go back to the moment itself.

sections.h2: How this gratitude meditation unfolds, room by room
p: The session opens gently. Your hands grow heavy, your fingers relax and you listen to the room without putting names on the sounds. Then you step into a museum with a few quiet rooms. Each one displays an ordinary moment from your recent days, the kind you would normally forget.

In the first room, you remember the first sip of a recent drink as a sensation, not an idea. In the second, a sound comes back, such as rain, a voice or laughter. The third holds something that simply worked, like a key that was right where you hoped it would be. You then picture the many unknown hands that made it possible. The excerpt at the top of this page takes you through these first three rooms.

Next comes the face of someone who eased your day a little, then one thing your body did for you, such as carrying you somewhere. A display case holds something lovely that nobody arranged for you, like sunlight across a table. A tiny fairy of light stops in front of it too.

A darker room holds a recent difficulty. You don’t have to be grateful for it, only to notice what helped you through. You thank your recent self for something that still helps you. Then you reach an almost empty room with a single chair: the place where you are now. To close, you hold one small moment in your palm like a tiny seed, then look around for one pleasant thing in the room.

sections.h2: When and how to practice gratitude meditation
p: “Daily Gratitude” lasts 14 minutes and is marked intermediate, yet it needs no special technique. If you can remember a sip of tea, you can follow it. It suits the end of the day well, since the rooms fill with moments from your day. In the morning, yesterday’s moments work just as well.

Sit or lie down, wherever your body feels supported. You can keep your eyes closed, since the session only asks you to look around at the very end. Headphones are optional. The opening invites you to hear the sounds of the room, so there is no need to shut them out.

sections.h2: What if your mind wanders or nothing comes?
p: Some rooms may feel full, others almost empty. That’s part of it, and the session leaves room for feeling nothing in particular. If no memory appears, pick something tiny, like a light that came on when you flipped the switch. Small is the point.

If your mind drifts to your to-do list, come back to the room you were in and to one detail of it. If you feel sleepy, sit up a little or open your eyes halfway. And if the darker room stirs some sadness, let it be there. You can stay with what helped you, or move on to the next room.

sections.h2: What to try after Daily Gratitude
p: In the same Emotional Growth category, “Compassion Meditation” takes 7 minutes and sends wishes of peace, first to yourself, then to others. “Developing Self-love”, 15 minutes, looks for a real quality in you, such as perseverance, and gives it a little love.
If you like writing things down, the Gratitude & Growth journal in the app has a “Daily Gratitude” section, where one line is enough. A good first line is the small moment you held in your palm.

faq: How do you do a gratitude meditation?

Settle in, then bring back one ordinary moment at a time and stay with its details: the taste, the sound, the face. In “Daily Gratitude”, each moment waits in its own room of an imaginary museum. At the end, you keep just one of them.
What if I don’t feel grateful?

That’s fine. The session never asks you to feel happy or thankful on command. Noticing a moment is enough, and some rooms may leave you with nothing in particular. You simply move on to the next one, without forcing a feeling.
Can I do a gratitude meditation every day?

Yes. A daily gratitude practice is easier to keep when it stays light, so choose a rhythm that suits you. The recording stays the same, but what you place in the rooms changes every day, because it comes from your own day.
Is a gratitude meditation the same as a gratitude journal?

No. A gratitude journal is written, while a gratitude meditation is listened to, often with your eyes closed. The two pair well: after the session, write down the small moment you held in your palm. One line is enough.

croiss05.seo: Forgiveness Meditation: How to Forgive Without Forgetting
croiss05.desc: Forgiveness meditation, 15 minutes, no pressure to forgive: on an old stone bridge, set down part of what you carry and keep what you learned. Free, no ads.
croiss05.h1: A guided forgiveness meditation: set down the stone, keep the lesson
croiss05.lead: This forgiveness meditation doesn’t ask you to forgive today. For 15 minutes, on an old stone bridge, you look at how much a past hurt still weighs on your body. You keep the lesson it taught you, then decide for yourself what you are ready to set down.

sections.h2: What does forgiveness mean in this meditation?
p: Before you reach the bridge, the session clears up three common mix-ups. Forgiving is not approving, it is not forgetting, and it gives no one permission to hurt you again.

Here, forgiveness is about the weight, not the memory. Each hurt becomes a stone in a bag on your shoulder: not the event itself, but what it still weighs today. You can set a stone down and keep the lesson, written on a small, light metal plate.
Recognizing the other person’s limits doesn’t excuse what they did. The session holds both at once: “Two truths can exist at the same time.” And the choice stays yours, at your own pace.

sections.h2: How the guided forgiveness meditation unfolds
p: You settle in and let your feet grow heavy. You notice your jaw, your neck and your hands, since an old hurt can live in the body as tension. Then you walk along an old path toward a stone bridge over a wide, slow river, with a bag of stones on your shoulder.

You pick someone who hurt you a little, not deeply, and place them far away on the other bank. You control the distance. You notice what happens in your body and give it a name, such as anger, sadness or a sense of injustice. A short sentence then reminds you that this reaction has a reason. The excerpt at the top of this page stops at that moment.

In the middle of the bridge, you put the bag down and start with one of the lighter stones. You name it and ask what you want to keep from this experience, such as a boundary to protect. Then you decide: leave the stone on the low wall, set it beside the path, or put it back in the bag.

Later, you see the other person as human, with fears and blind spots. You remember that the event is a memory, not something happening now, and a gentle shower of light falls on the river. One stone may bear your own name: a part of this story you still hold against yourself. This step borrows from self-compassion exercises: you judge who you were by what you could really do back then.
Finally, you close the bag, which this session never sets out to empty, and cross the rest of the bridge toward your own path, not toward the person.

sections.h2: Who it is for and when to practice
p: This session is for you if you still carry an old hurt, whether or not you want to forgive. It lasts 15 minutes and is marked intermediate. Start with a hurt of medium weight, as the session suggests, rather than the deepest one.

Choose a quiet moment when no one needs you for a quarter of an hour. Sit on a chair or on the floor, or lie on a bed: the session mentions all three. Headphones are optional, though they can help you stay on the bridge in a noisy home.

sections.h2: What if anger rises or your mind drifts?
p: Strong feelings may come up. The session shows how to process your emotions in that moment: feel where they sit in your body, name them, and remember that they have a reason. Keep the person as far away as you need. You can also open your eyes and stop.

If a memory feels too present, come back to what is here, as the session does: the stone under your feet, the air on your skin. If your mind drifts into the old story, return to the weight of the bag. And if you are not ready to let go of a stone, put it back. That is a real choice, not a failure.

Forgiving never means staying close to someone who harms you. If the hurt is recent or still going on, protecting yourself comes first, and talking with someone you trust or with a professional can help.

sections.h2: What to try after this forgiveness meditation
p: In the same Emotional Growth category, “Welcoming a Difficult Emotion”, 17 minutes, is a good next step when anger or sadness stays with you. “Compassion Meditation”, 7 minutes, sends wishes of peace to yourself first, then to others.
If the stone with your own name felt heavy, “Forgiving Yourself”, in the Shadow & Well-being category, gives it a whole session.

faq: Do I have to forgive the person who hurt me?

No. The session says so from the start, and it never pushes. You explore what forgiving would mean for you, then choose what to set down and what to keep. Putting a stone back in the bag is a valid choice too.
Can you forgive without forgetting?

Yes. In this meditation, the memory stays and the lesson stays, while part of the weight is set down. Forgiving does not mean approving what happened, and it gives no one permission to do it again. You can remember without carrying the full weight.
What if I’m not ready to forgive?

Then you put the stone back and cross the bridge with your bag. The session treats being able to choose as part of forgiveness. You can come back another day and start with a smaller stone, at your own pace.
Is this also a self-forgiveness meditation?

Partly. Most of the session looks at someone who hurt you, with one step for the self-blame that can hide in the same story. For a full self-forgiveness meditation, “Forgiving Yourself”, in the Shadow & Well-being category, lasts 17 minutes.

ombre04.seo: Self-Forgiveness Meditation: How to Process Guilt Gently
ombre04.desc: Self-forgiveness meditation, 17 minutes: face a mistake from three chairs, own your part, then set down the self-blame you keep carrying. Free, no ads.
ombre04.h1: Forgiving yourself: a self-forgiveness meditation in three chairs
ombre04.lead: In this self-forgiveness meditation, you look at a mistake without excusing it and without condemning yourself. Over 17 minutes, in a bare room with three chairs, you say what happened, separate your part from the rest, and look for one real thing you can repair.

sections.h2: What does it mean to forgive yourself?
p: Forgiving yourself doesn’t mean deciding the mistake didn’t matter. In this session, it means telling responsibility apart from repeated self-blame. Responsibility looks at what happened and asks what can be repaired. Self-blame replays the scene and keeps you frozen inside it.

The session pictures that self-blame as a weight your past self holds against their chest, like a dark stone. You don’t throw it away or pretend it isn’t there. You lift it together and set it on the floor, so you no longer carry it every moment.
This is self-compassion in a very concrete form. A neutral witness neither excuses you nor crushes you, and in the end tells you: “You can be responsible and still go on living.”

sections.h2: How to process guilt, step by step
p: You start by feeling your back as points of contact, from the pelvis up to the back of your head, and your ribs widening as you breathe in. Then you choose a regret you can bear to look at, not necessarily the most painful one.

In a simple room with daylight, you sit in the first chair, the seat of who you are today. Your past self appears in the second. Before speaking, you notice your chest, your jaw and your hands. Then you say what happened in one plain sentence, without excuses or insults, and let silence follow. The excerpt at the top of this page stops right there.

You ask what your past self knew at the time, and what they had not yet learned. A third chair appears, and a neutral witness sits down. You tell them the facts, check your breath after each sentence, and keep your back against the chair instead of shrinking.

The witness asks what truly belongs to you in this story, and what does not, like other people’s choices. Then you look for one real repair, such as an apology or a new limit. Sometimes the honest answer is that direct repair is no longer possible. You stop the image before the other person answers, because their response is not yours.

You set the weight down together, walk out of the room side by side, and feel your past self return to their place in a larger story. With one hand on your chest, you end with four short phrases, one breath each, the last one giving you permission to continue.

sections.h2: Who this self-forgiveness meditation is for
p: It’s for anyone who keeps replaying a mistake, big or small, long after it happened. It lasts 17 minutes and is marked intermediate. In the Shadow & Well-being category, it is a gentle piece of shadow work: you turn toward a part of your story you would rather avoid.

Give yourself a quiet moment, with a little free time afterward. Lie on your back or sit against a high backrest, since the opening moves through the points where your back meets the support. Headphones are optional. A calm room matters more.

sections.h2: What if shame gets heavy or your mind wanders?
p: Shame often pulls the body inward, as if to hide. When that happens, feel your back against the support and notice your breath, as the session does after each sentence. You can open your eyes and stop at any time, or choose a lighter memory next time.

If your mind slips into long explanations or self-criticism, come back to one plain sentence of facts. If you feel sleepy, sit up a little. When shame returns later in the day, the session leaves you one simple tool: repeat its last phrase a single time.
If guilt weighs on your days for a long time, talking with someone you trust or with a professional is a good step too.

sections.h2: Shadow work exercises to try next
p: In the same category, “Fear of Failure”, 10 minutes, separates what happened from what you conclude about yourself. “Shadow Work”, 17 minutes, lets you meet a difficult part of yourself and see what it is trying to protect.
If someone else hurt you, “Forgiving Without Forgetting”, in the Emotional Growth category, uses a bridge and a bag of stones to explore forgiveness at your own pace.

faq: How do you forgive yourself for a mistake?

Look at it plainly, without excuses or insults, and name your part. Then repair what you can and set down the self-blame that keeps repeating. In this session, a neutral witness helps you separate what belongs to you from what doesn’t.
Does forgiving yourself mean the mistake didn’t matter?

No. The session is clear on this point: nothing is erased. You acknowledge the mistake, learn from it, and repair what can be repaired. What you put down is the self-blame that keeps replaying, not the responsibility.
How do you process emotions like guilt and shame?

Start with the body: notice where they sit, in the chest, the jaw or the hands. Then state the facts in one plain sentence and separate your part from what isn’t yours. Shame tends to make you shrink, so keep your back supported.
Is self-forgiveness the same as self-compassion?

They’re close. Self-compassion is a kind way of treating yourself in hard moments, and self-forgiveness applies it to one specific mistake. This session works like a self-compassion meditation aimed at a single regret, with a witness who neither excuses nor crushes you.

ombre07.seo: Fear of Abandonment: A Gentle 10-Minute Guided Meditation
ombre07.desc: Fear of abandonment, met gently: a 10-minute guided meditation with one hand on your chest, on a quiet platform where trains come and go. Free, no ads.
ombre07.h1: A meditation for the fear of abandonment, one hand on your chest
ombre07.lead: Fear of abandonment is the fear that the people you count on will leave, or stop caring. This 10-minute meditation doesn’t argue with it. From a quiet platform, one hand on your chest, you watch it pass like a train, and you stay.

sections.h2: What is fear of abandonment?
p: Fear of abandonment is the fear of being left: that someone close will go away, go silent or stop caring. Many people feel it at times. Small things can stir it up, like a reply that takes too long, a door that closes or a goodbye.

It often shows up in the body: a tight belly, a lump in the throat, a pressure in the chest. Then come the urges: to call out, to cling or to make yourself very small. For many people, the fear feels older than the moment that sets it off. That’s why the session invites a younger version of you to sit beside you.
If you are learning how to process emotions like this one, the body is a good place to start. You feel the fear before you act on it.

sections.h2: How the fear of abandonment meditation works
p: You settle into a well-supported position. One hand goes to the center of your chest and the other to your belly, or you hug yourself gently. Reassurance can wait. For now, you only feel the contact, its weight and its warmth.

Then you picture yourself waiting on the platform of a little station. Each passing train carries an image linked to the fear, like someone slow to reply or someone walking away. You watch through the window, notice your real body and leave your hands in place. You never board.

A younger you then sits beside you. You rest an imagined hand on their back and keep your real hand on yourself, which is where the excerpt at the top of this page ends. You promise only what you can keep: “I’ll stay with you while this passes.”

A more personal train goes by, with an absence or a silence, and you let it pass. Then you bring to mind someone ordinary who is still in your life. The part of you that spots every absence gets to notice presence too.

You try two short sentences about someone leaving and keep the one that feels more believable. A last train passes while you mostly feel your feet, your pelvis and your hands. You stay until your belly softens under your palm.

sections.h2: A guided meditation for anxiety about being left
p: Use it when the fear is awake, for example while you wait for a reply. You can also practice on a calm day, to get to know the platform before you need it. The session lasts 10 minutes and is marked intermediate.

Sit or lie down in a position where your hands rest on you without effort, such as lying on your back or sitting against a cushion. Close your eyes if that feels safe, or lower your gaze. Headphones are optional, but a quiet spot helps.
The session doesn’t fight the fear. It works as a short self-compassion meditation: a hand that stays while the feeling passes.

sections.h2: What if the fear grows during the session?
p: The feeling may linger a few seconds after a train leaves. The session expects this. Let it fade at its own pace and come back to the weight of your hand. If an image feels too strong, look at it less, as you do with the last train.
If your mind starts writing stories about what someone meant, return to the touch on your chest. If tears come, let them. You can open your eyes, look around the room and stop whenever you need to.

Fear of abandonment is a human feeling, not a label to put on yourself. If it takes up a lot of room in your relationships, talking with someone you trust or with a professional can be a real support.

sections.h2: Shadow work sessions to try next
p: This session belongs to Shadow & Well-being, where shadow work means turning gently toward feelings you usually avoid. “Inner Child Serenity”, 19 minutes, returns to the younger you through play and safety. “Fear of Failure”, 10 minutes, looks at another common fear with the same care.

faq: How do I calm my anxiety when someone doesn’t reply?

Start with your body before your phone. Put one hand on your chest and one on your belly, and feel their weight. Notice the tightness, let the wave pass, then decide what to do. That is the core gesture of this session.
Is fear of abandonment common?

Yes. Many people feel it at some point, especially when a relationship changes or someone pulls away. It can be a passing jolt or a fear that shapes how you love. This meditation meets it gently, without labels or judgment.
Can this meditation make the fear go away?

It doesn’t promise that. The session even points out that no one can promise people will never leave. What it offers is a way to stay present with yourself while the fear rises and passes, with your hands as an anchor.
Why does the session bring in a younger version of me?

Because this fear often feels older than the situation that sets it off, like a child’s fear. With one imagined hand on your younger self’s back and one real hand on you, you offer the presence that part of you is looking for.

ombre08.seo: Fear of Failure: A 10-Minute Meditation for Anxiety
ombre08.desc: Fear of failure, seen up close: a 10-minute meditation for anxiety about failing. Sort what happened from what you conclude, then picture a first version.
ombre08.h1: Fear of failure: a guided meditation in the workshop of first versions
ombre08.lead: Fear of failure is the dread that a bad result would prove something about you. In this 10-minute meditation, you practice telling two things apart: what actually happened, and what a frightened part of you concludes about your worth.

sections.h2: What is fear of failure?
p: Fear of failure is the fear that failing would say something about you: that you are not good enough, that people will see you differently, or that you don’t deserve your place. It often looks like caution. You check everything twice, start over, or hesitate to begin at all.
The session treats this fear as a part of you with a job. It may be trying to protect you from shame, criticism or disappointment. It works hard, and its shoulders are probably tired.

The heart of the practice is a simple difference. “I failed” is a fact about an attempt. “I am a failure” is a verdict about a person. On days when you feel you have no self-confidence at all, that feeling may be one more verdict.

sections.h2: How the fear of failure meditation unfolds
p: You settle, feel your feet and bring the word “failure” to mind. You notice where it lands, in your belly, your chest or your shoulders. Then you rephrase it: a part of you is afraid of failing. The fear is still there, but it takes up less space.

You picture a workshop full of tools and early versions. The part that fears failing works there, checking everything. It shows you a pile of rejected objects, each with a harsh label, like “clumsy” or “too late.” You ask what role it plays and listen without arguing. You also ask what it believes a failure would say about you. The excerpt at the top of this page goes as far as the moment you pick up one object from the pile.

Looked at again, that object may be an attempt, a piece of information or a step. A phoenix lands on the windowsill, its feathers glowing like embers. Then you set two labels on the table: what happened, and what you conclude about yourself.

You recall a minor setback and file the bare facts under the first label. You watch what the fearful part adds under the second. The facts may be true, while the verdict is only one view. You ask the part whether it would still need to frighten you without that second label. A tiny fairy lands on the pile and sees an attempt, not a failure.

Turning over early versions, you find the words “Version 1,” then “Version 2,” then “Version 3.” The workshop turns out to be a place for making things, not a court. The part may keep its eye for detail, as long as it works without blame. You picture the first, imperfect version of something you want to try, and you leave with one small label: “Next version.”

sections.h2: A 10-minute meditation for anxiety about failing
p: Use it before something that scares you, like an exam, a launch or a hard conversation. Or use it after a setback, while the facts are still tangled with the verdict. It lasts 10 minutes and is marked intermediate.

Sit in a stable position with your feet on the floor, or lie down if you prefer. Close your eyes or lower your gaze. Headphones are optional. If you wonder how to start shadow work, a short session on one fear, like this one, is a gentle first step.

sections.h2: What if the fear gets louder or your mind wanders?
p: The fearful part may not go quiet, and the session says so. Look instead for a small change, like a chest or belly that loosens a little. If a real failure still feels too fresh, choose a smaller one, as the session suggests.

If your mind runs off to plans and fixes, come back to the object in your hands, or to the place where the word landed in your body. If old shame comes up, you can pause, open your eyes and breathe. Nothing in the workshop needs to be finished today.

sections.h2: What to try after Fear of Failure
p: In the same Shadow & Well-being category, “Fear of Judgment”, 7 minutes, loosens the feeling of being watched. “Releasing Fear”, 16 minutes, sits you beside a sentinel that has guarded a door for a very long time.
For self-confidence built on evidence, “Building Self-Confidence Through Evidence and Action”, in the Emotional Growth category, takes 6 minutes.

faq: How do you overcome the fear of failure?

There is no switch to flip, but there are small steps. One is to separate what happened from what you conclude about yourself. Another is to try a modest, imperfect first version and learn from it. This session practices both in 10 minutes.
Is fear of failure the same as perfectionism?

Not exactly, but they often travel together. Perfectionism sets the bar very high, while fear of failure dreads what missing it would say about you. In the session, the part that checks everything keeps its eye for detail but stops deciding your worth.
Why does the session talk to a part of me?

Because a fear is easier to look at when it doesn’t fill your whole self. Naming it as one part leaves room for the rest of you. Then you can ask that part what job it believes it has, and listen without arguing.
Is this a free 10-minute meditation?

Yes. “Fear of Failure” is a free 10-minute guided meditation for anxiety about failing, in the MeditaDream app. There are no ads and no account to create, and once downloaded, the session plays offline.

tradi01.seo: How to Do Vipassana Meditation: A Guided First Session
tradi01.desc: How to do vipassana meditation: sit still, follow your belly as it rises and falls, and note each sensation with one quiet word. A 7-minute guided start.
tradi01.h1: How to do vipassana meditation, one quiet label at a time
tradi01.lead: Here is how to do vipassana meditation: sit still, follow the rise and fall of your belly, and note each experience with one quiet word, such as “thinking” or “hearing.” This short guided session walks you through it and lets you watch each sensation change.

sections.h2: What is vipassana in Buddhism?
p: Vipassana is a Pali word usually translated as “insight” or “clear seeing.” It is the insight meditation of Theravada Buddhism, the form of Buddhism found in Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Thailand. That tradition traces it back to the Buddha’s teachings on mindfulness.

The practice is simple to describe. You observe what happens in your body and mind as it happens, and you notice that it keeps changing. The aim is not to reach a special state, only to look closely at sensations and the way they shift.

Schools differ in style. The noting used here, with its “rising” and “falling,” is associated with the Burmese teacher Mahasi Sayadaw. The ten-day courses of S. N. Goenka teach a slow scan of the body instead. Both belong to the same family of Buddhist meditation.

sections.h2: How to do vipassana meditation, step by step
p: Sit in a stable position and bring your attention to your belly. Breathe naturally. As it rises, silently note “rising.” As it falls, note “falling.”
When you get lost, name what pulled you away with one quiet word: “thinking” for plans, “imagining” for a scene, “hearing” for a sound. Then come back to the belly.

Next, pick a sensation you can feel clearly, such as pressure, warmth or tingling. Notice where it is and what it feels like, without telling a story about it. It may grow, fade or stay steady. Note, too, whether it is pleasant, unpleasant or neutral. A wish for more comfort becomes “wanting,” and pushing away becomes “resisting.”

Then you look more closely at one sensation, such as the place where your hand meets your leg. You explore where the pressure starts and whether one spot feels warmer, without needing answers in words. The excerpt at the top of this page covers everything up to this point.

A sound becomes “hearing,” and any irritation that follows becomes “unpleasant” or “resisting.” In the words of the session, “The sound and your reaction are different events.” Telling them apart lets you recognize an experience instead of reacting on autopilot.

To finish, you return to the belly for two breaths. You note “seeing” as you open your eyes and “moving” as your hand moves. Afterward, everyday acts like walking or opening a door can become brief chances to observe before you interpret.

sections.h2: When and how to sit for vipassana
p: Sit on a chair, a cushion or a meditation bench, with your back upright but not stiff. Rest your hands on your thighs: the session uses that contact later. You can close your eyes, as the session only has you open them at the very end.

The session lasts 7 minutes and is marked intermediate, yet it works well as a first taste. A quiet room helps, but you don’t need silence, because sounds become part of the practice. Headphones are optional. Morning, a lunch break or the end of the day all work.

sections.h2: What if your mind wanders or your body protests?
p: Your mind will wander, and that is part of the method. Each time you notice it and name it, you are practicing. Keep the label soft, almost a whisper, and come back to the belly without judging yourself.

If a sensation feels like too much, the session invites you to open your eyes, change position and rest your attention on something neutral. Vipassana doesn’t ask you to sit through real pain. If you feel drowsy, straighten your back or let a little light in through half-open eyes.
Strong feelings can surface too. Note an unpleasant wave as “unpleasant,” feel where it sits, then go back to your breath.

sections.h2: Where to go after this first taste of vipassana
p: In the same World Meditations category, Shamatha — Tibet: Cultivating Clear, Stable Attention, 6 minutes, invites you to rest your attention on a single point, as taught in Tibetan Buddhism. “Seon and Hwadu” — Korea: Staying With a Living Question, 6 minutes, offers a taste of Korean Seon, the counterpart of Japanese Zen meditation.

faq: How long should vipassana meditation last?

Start with a few minutes, like this session, then add time gradually as it feels easier. On residential retreats, people sit for many hours a day, but a short daily practice at home is already a real beginning.
What should I do when my mind wanders?

Note it with one word, such as “thinking” or “imagining,” then come back to the rise and fall of your belly. Wandering is not a mistake in vipassana. Each time you notice it, you are doing the practice itself.
Do I need to be Buddhist to practice vipassana?

No. Vipassana comes from Buddhism, and meditation as practiced here asks for no belief: you only observe your breath, your sensations and your reactions. People of every faith, or of none, practice it this way.
Is vipassana the same as Zen meditation?

No, though both come from Buddhism. In vipassana, from the Theravada tradition, you watch sensations and thoughts change moment by moment. Zen meditation, rooted in Chan and Japanese Buddhism, centers on sitting and simply being present.
Is this the same as the Buddha’s vipassana meditation?

It is a short introduction in that tradition, not a full course. Theravada schools trace vipassana to the Buddha’s teachings on mindfulness. This session gives you its core gesture: noting each experience as it arises and changes.

trance06.seo: Past Life Meditation: Step Through a Door Into Another Era
trance06.desc: A guided past life meditation, lying down: step through doors into other eras, glide upriver through time and imagine past lives. No belief required.
trance06.h1: A past life meditation in the corridor of a thousand doors
trance06.lead: This past life meditation is a journey of the imagination, not a test of whether you lived before. Lying down for about 20 minutes, you picture a corridor lined with doors and step into scenes from other eras. Then you come back to your present life with a single trace of the journey.

sections.h2: What happens in this past life meditation
p: You lie down and let your shoulders, jaw and hands go soft. The ceiling and walls seem to drift away. You find yourself in a long, warmly lit corridor lined with more doors than you could ever count. You walk until your body reacts to one of them. The excerpt above lets you hear this opening.

Behind that door, you don’t start by guessing the year. You put the scene together layer by layer, starting with your feet, clothes and hands. Then come the light, sounds and smells. The era comes last, taking shape from those clues. You watch people going about their day, then step back into the corridor. This first visit is a warm-up.

Another door opens onto a river. A boat with no oars carries you upstream on its own. Along the banks, time runs backward: cities turn into villages, then fields, then forest. You step out onto pale sand and walk down a bare stone corridor. A door that lets white light through opens onto a narrow street, then a market.

There, someone greets you, and you notice how your body responds before you choose who this person is. In a cool building, you rest your hands on a work surface and wait for a single gesture to come. You repeat it without drawing conclusions. Then the river carries you back downstream to the first corridor. At the last door, which opens onto your present life, you hold one sensation from the journey in your hand. The voice is clear that this isn’t proof: “Only a trace.” Finally, you feel your body again. The corridor stays there if you want to linger.

sections.h2: What are past lives?
p: The idea of past lives comes from reincarnation, the belief that a person has lived before and will live again. It runs through several traditions. Hinduism and Buddhism describe a cycle of rebirth. In ancient Greece, thinkers such as Plato wrote of souls returning in new lives. No one can confirm or rule out a past life, so it remains a matter of belief.

People also mention past lives when a period, a country or a craft feels oddly familiar. This past life meditation doesn’t settle the question. It makes clear from the start that the doors belong to your imagination. You can treat it as a way to explore that feeling, or simply as a waking dream set in history.

sections.h2: Who is this session for, and how do you get comfortable?
p: This advanced session suits people who already practice guided meditation. It invites a light trance, the kind of absorption you may know from a good novel. Absorption like this is one of the most common altered states of consciousness. If trance is new to you, start with “Progressive Descent into Trance”, which teaches you to go down in stages.

Pick a quiet time when nothing is waiting for you afterward. Lie on a bed, a couch or a mat, somewhere no one will interrupt you. A pillow under your knees eases your lower back, and headphones help you stay with the voice. Never listen while driving or doing anything that needs your full attention.

sections.h2: What if no images come, or a strong feeling does?
p: Seeing few or no images is common, especially at first. The session starts with small details, like the ground under your feet or the nearest sound. It never asks for a full story. In its own words: “One precise gesture may matter more than an invented life story.” If your mind wanders, come back to your feet or your hands inside the scene. If you keep drifting off to sleep, raise your head a little.

A place or a gesture can stir up emotion. Let it pass as you breathe. If it feels like too much, open your eyes and come back to the weight of your body. Afterward, don’t rush to decide what it all meant. The meaning sometimes comes later.

sections.h2: What to try after this past life meditation
p: If the gesture stayed with you, try “Forgotten Talents”. At 16 minutes, it’s the shortest session in the category. You step into the shoes of a craftsperson from long ago and bring one quality back with you. “Past Lives & Time” follows a different thread, your family line. You decide what to keep, what to set down and what to pass on.

faq: Can a meditation reveal your past lives?

Not in any way anyone can check, and this one doesn’t claim to. It invites you to imagine a scene from another era and notice what your body seems to recognize, or doesn’t. What you bring back is a personal experience to reflect on, not evidence of a previous life.
Do I have to believe in reincarnation?

No. The session asks for no particular belief. Everything behind its doors is something you imagine. You can approach it as a spiritual exploration, a curious look at other eras or practice in noticing sensations. Whether or not you believe in past lives, you simply observe what comes.
Is this a past life regression meditation?

Not in the usual sense. Past life regression is typically done under hypnosis, with a practitioner who guides you and asks what you see. Here there’s no back-and-forth: you follow the voice in the app and can open your eyes at any time. The journey isn’t meant to recover memories. It unfolds in your imagination.
Does this session teach you how to remember past lives?

No, and it makes no such promise. Rather than having you search for past life memories, it asks you to build each scene through your senses. It also asks you not to look for a message. Whatever comes, familiar or not, the meaning you give it is yours.
How long is the session, and does it work offline?

It runs about 20 minutes. You only need a connection to download it the first time. After that, it plays offline, even in airplane mode. It’s one of 144 guided meditations in MeditaDream, a free app with no ads and no account.
